proposals.before: In Long'an 4 (AD 400), he claimed the imperial title at the southern suburban altar, issued a general amnesty, inaugurated the Jianping era, established a traveling ancestral temple south of the palace, and sent envoys bearing the accession proclamation.
proposals.after: In Long'an 4 (AD 400), at the southern suburb he assumed the imperial throne—an act the history presents as usurpation—issued a general amnesty, adopted the Jianping era name, established a temporary ancestral temple south of the palace, and sent envoys with a document to report the accomplishment there.
proposals.reason: Revise to restore the locative 焉, read as the immediately preceding temporary temple; this antecedent is plausible but interpretative. Attribute the evaluative 僭 to the history, not objective fact. Keep the document and reported accomplishment unspecified. The AD conversion in the idiomatic field remains unaudited.

proposals.before: Later at a banquet for his ministers, when the wine was warm he laughed and said, 'Though I am meager, I reverently face south to court the lords; not proud on high, anxious at my post by night; with whom among the ancients may I be compared?'
proposals.after: Later at a banquet for his ministers, when the wine was warm he laughed and said, 'Though I am meager, I conduct myself respectfully, face south, and receive the lords at court; not proud on high, anxious at my post by night; with whom among the ancients may I be compared?'
proposals.reason: 恭己南面而朝諸侯 depicts the south-facing ruler receiving the lords at court, not him courting them; the remaining inherited wording is not assessed by this focused repair.

proposals.before: Thereupon he took Yan Mo along to the temple of Prince Jing of Chengyang at Hancheng, feasted the common elders at Shen Pool, climbed north Mount Sheshou, looked east at the tripod legs of terrain, then gazed at Mount Niu and sighed, saying, 'From antiquity there has been no not dying!'
proposals.after: Thereupon he took Yan Mo along to the temple of Han Prince Jing of Chengyang, feasted the common elders at Shen Pool, climbed north Mount Sheshou, looked east at the tripod legs of terrain, then gazed at Mount Niu and sighed, saying, 'From antiquity there has been no not dying!'
proposals.reason: 漢 identifies the Han dynasty, not the place Hancheng. The proposal only changes this phrase; the remainder needs separate review.

proposals.before: He opened ironworks on Mount Shang and salt monopolies at Wuchang Marsh to swell the army's coffers.
proposals.after: He established smelting works on Mount Shang and a salt office at Wuchang Marsh to increase resources for the army and the state.
proposals.reason: The source specifies smelting and a salt administration for military and state use, but not iron, monopolies, or army coffers.

proposals.before: A eunuch helped Murong De over the wall into hiding.
proposals.after: Palace attendant Xun Jin helped De over the wall, and De hid at Jin's residence.
proposals.reason: 遜進 is the personal name Xun Jin; 進舍 is his residence. The subject of the second clause is rendered as De, without inventing Xun Jin as the agent of hiding.

proposals.before: Palace attendant Xun Jin helped De over the wall and hid him in a forward lodging.
proposals.after: Palace attendant Xun Jin helped De over the wall, and De hid at Jin's residence.
proposals.reason: 遜進 is the personal name Xun Jin; 進舍 is his residence. The subject of the second clause is rendered as De, without inventing Xun Jin as the agent of hiding.

proposals.before: Duan Hong and the rest heard the alarm and sealed the four gates with troops.
proposals.after: Duan Hong and the others heard of the palace disturbance and stationed their troops at the four gates.
proposals.reason: The source places troops at the four gates but does not say they were sealed. 勒兵 also suggests mustering or commanding troops; this narrow correction does not resolve that nuance.

proposals.before: Murong De re-entered the palace, executed Hou Chimei's faction, and Murong Da fled to Wei.
proposals.after: Murong De entered the palace and executed Hou Chimei and the others; Murong Da fled in fear to Wei.
proposals.reason: 赤眉等 means Chimei and others, not necessarily a faction; 達懼 expressly gives Da’s fear. Names follow the immediately preceding context.

proposals.before: Sui replied, 'King Wu of Zhou closed Bi Gan's tomb, Han's Gaozu sacrificed at Lord Xinling's grave—both fixed their hearts on worthies and often cherished old deeds.
proposals.after: Sui replied, 'King Wu of Zhou raised a mound over Bi Gan's tomb, Han's Gaozu sacrificed at Lord Xinling's grave—both fixed their hearts on worthies and often cherished old deeds.
proposals.reason: In 武王封比干之墓, the transmitted gloss 積土為封 explains heaping earth over the tomb; “closed” wrongly suggests sealing the tomb rather than the commemorative mound action.

proposals.before: Spanning several thousand li, hosts exceeding a hundred thousand, we could west merge with strong Qin and north resist Great Wei.
proposals.after: Spanning several thousand li with a host exceeding a hundred thousand, we could annex strong Qin to the west and resist Great Wei to the north.
proposals.reason: 西並強秦 describes annexing Qin, not merging with it by agreement.

proposals.reason: 西並強秦 describes annexing Qin, not merging with it by agreement.

proposals.before: He staged a review west of the city with hundreds of thousands on parade.
proposals.after: He reviewed his forces west of the city: 370,000 infantry, 17,000 vehicles, and 53,000 armored cavalry. They stretched across the mountains and marshes, their banners filled the landscape, and the sound of gongs and drums shook heaven and earth.
proposals.reason: Restore the reported troop and vehicle figures and visual and sound details; these are the text’s figures, not an independently verified count. Vehicles avoids deciding the exact type of 車.

proposals.before: De climbed high and looked over them, and said to Liu Gui and Gao Yazhi, 'Formerly Xi Ke avenged Qi, Wu Zixu resented Chu, and in the end they could vent their fierce integrity and their names flow a thousand years.
proposals.after: De climbed high and looked over them, and said to Liu Gui and Gao Yazhi, 'Formerly Xi Ke took vengeance on Qi, Wu Zixu resented Chu, and in the end they could vent their fierce integrity and their names flow a thousand years.
proposals.reason: 仇齊 makes Qi the object of Xi Ke’s hostility, not the injured party whom he avenged. Other wording remains for separate review.

proposals.reason: 仇齊 makes Qi the object of Xi Ke’s hostility, not the injured party whom he avenged. Other wording remains for separate review.

proposals.before: Thereupon he issued an edict making Chao crown prince, amnestied the realm, and for sons continuing fathers raised each man's rank two grades.
proposals.after: Thereupon he issued an edict making Chao crown prince and granting an amnesty throughout the realm; sons succeeding their fathers were each granted two grades of rank.
proposals.reason: The rank grant does not require a prior rank; match the independently revised idiomatic field without asserting an increase.

proposals.before: They ran decoy coffers out each gate and hid his true burial in the hills.
proposals.after: That night they prepared more than ten coffins and sent them out through the four gates, burying him secretly in the mountain valleys; in the end, no one knew where his body lay.
proposals.reason: 棺 means coffins, not coffers; preserve the number, nocturnal setting and uncertain location. The text does not explicitly identify any particular coffin as a decoy.

proposals.before: His temple posthumous title was Emperor Xianwu.
proposals.after: His posthumous title was Emperor Xianwu, a title this history treats as illegitimate.
proposals.reason: 諡 is the posthumous designation, not a temple name. 偽 expresses this history's claim of illegitimacy; the proposed 'Jin historian' risks misidentifying the compiler's period. Zizhi Tongjian 114 separately distinguishes 諡獻武皇帝 from 廟號世宗.

proposals.before: He was posthumously titled Emperor Xianwu.
proposals.after: His posthumous title was Emperor Xianwu, a title this history treats as illegitimate.
proposals.reason: 偽 expresses the source's judgment of illegitimacy, while 諡 is a posthumous title. Avoid 'the Jin historian': the Book of Jin is a later compilation, so that label misleadingly suggests an author from the Jin period. The wording attributes the judgment to this history rather than endorsing it.

proposals.before: He founded an academy with two hundred students from elite families.
proposals.after: He established educational offices and chose 200 students for the Imperial Academy from among the sons and younger brothers of officials from dukes and ministers on down, and young men from scholar families of the second rank.
proposals.reason: The Chinese distinguishes descendants of dukes, ministers and officials below them from a second group, scholar families of the second rank. It selects two hundred students across the groups. The rank qualifies the family in the second group. Liang Ruixue discusses this sentence explicitly on PDF page 30.

proposals.before: He established schools, selecting two hundred sons of dukes and ministers down to second rank gentry households as academy students.
proposals.after: He established educational offices and selected two hundred from among the sons and younger brothers of the dukes and ministers and those below them, and from scholar families of the second rank, to be students at the Imperial Academy.
proposals.reason: The Chinese distinguishes descendants of dukes, ministers and officials below them from a second group, scholar families of the second rank. It selects two hundred students across the groups. The rank qualifies the family in the second group. Liang Ruixue discusses this sentence explicitly on PDF page 30.

proposals.before: De said, 'I am now scattering the wealth I lightly esteem to recruit the deaths I heavily value; how could I be stingy for a revered kinsman?
proposals.after: De said, 'I am giving away wealth, which I value little, to enlist a man willing to die in my service, which I value greatly. How could I begrudge such a gift for a revered parent?
proposals.reason: Du Hong has offered to risk death on his mission and asked for a stipend for his father. 散所輕之財 and 招所重之死 contrast wealth that De readily gives away with the willingness to die that he prizes. 親尊 is left as a revered parent without supplying a possessor. The quotation continues in s0195.

proposals.before: De said, 'I am now scattering the wealth I lightly esteem to recruit the deaths I heavily value; how could I be stingy for a revered kinsman?
proposals.after: De said, 'I am distributing wealth, which I hold lightly, to enlist service even unto death, which I prize. How could I be stingy when it is for a revered parent?
proposals.reason: Du Hong has offered to risk death on his mission and asked for a stipend for his father. 散所輕之財 and 招所重之死 contrast wealth that De readily gives away with the willingness to die that he prizes. 親尊 is left as a revered parent without supplying a possessor. The quotation continues in s0195.

proposals.before: Murong Chao, his elder brother's son, whom he had summoned from Chang'an, now arrived.
proposals.after: Murong De had earlier sent for his elder brother's son Murong Chao in Chang'an. Chao now arrived.
proposals.reason: The current wording restores the kinship and the two stages of the journey. The parallel in Jinshu 128 explicitly says that De sent an envoy to meet Chao. ‘Sent for’ leaves open whether De issued a formal summons.

proposals.before: Earlier, De had summoned his elder brother's son Chao from Chang'an; at this point he arrived.
proposals.after: Earlier, De had sent for his elder brother's son Chao in Chang'an. At this point Chao arrived.
proposals.reason: The current wording preserves the elder-brother relationship. Jinshu 128 describes an envoy sent to meet Chao. ‘Sent for’ expresses the earlier action and naming Chao makes clear who arrived.

proposals.before: He issued an edict naming Murong Chao crown prince, proclaimed a general amnesty within his realm, and raised by two degrees the rank of every son who was his father’s heir.
proposals.after: He issued an edict naming Murong Chao crown prince, proclaimed a general amnesty within his realm, and granted two grades of rank to each son who succeeded his father.
proposals.reason: The current wording restores both the edict and the rank provision. 人爵二級 specifies the award to each heir and gives no initial rank for the recipients. ‘Granted two grades of rank’ preserves the award without assuming that every recipient held rank already.

proposals.before: Before he came of age he already stood eight feet two inches tall, cut an imposing figure, and bore the paired “sun-brow” and “crescent moon” lines on his forehead that physiognomists read as imperial signs.
proposals.after: Before he came of age he already stood eight chi and two cun tall, cut an imposing figure, and bore the paired “sun-brow” and “crescent moon” lines on his forehead that physiognomists read as imperial signs.
proposals.reason: 八尺二寸 measures eight chi and two cun. The literal field preserves the two source units. Their numerical values cannot be carried into modern feet and inches without a sourced conversion.

proposals.before: He named Murong Lin minister of works and chief of the secretariat, Murong Fa central-army general, Yu Ba senior vice-president of the secretariat, Ding Tong junior vice-president, and distributed other posts accordingly.
proposals.after: He appointed Murong Lin minister of works and concurrent director of the Secretariat, Murong Fa general of the central army, Muyu Ba left vice-director of the Secretariat, and Ding Tong right vice-director. The others received titles and appointments of varying rank.
proposals.reason: 慕輿拔 has the compound surname Muyu, also spelled out in s0178. The two Secretariat offices are explicitly left and right, and 自余封授各有差 covers the other grants and appointments.

proposals.before: Murong De appointed Murong Lin as minister of works and concurrent director of the secretariat, Murong Fa as general of the central army, Yu Ba as left vice-director of the secretariat, Ding Tong as right vice-director of the secretariat, and the rest received titles each according to rank.
proposals.after: Murong De appointed Murong Lin as minister of works and concurrent director of the secretariat, Murong Fa as general of the central army, Muyu Ba as left vice-director of the secretariat, Ding Tong as right vice-director of the secretariat, and the rest received titles each according to rank.
proposals.reason: The full Chinese name 慕輿拔 includes both characters of the surname 慕輿. The later appointment in s0178 already uses Muyu Ba.

proposals.before: Yu Hu volunteered to ride north and learn Murong Bao's true situation; Murong De sent him off in tears.
proposals.after: Muyu Hu volunteered to ride out and learn Murong Bao's true situation. Murong De sent him off in tears.
proposals.reason: 慕輿護 is Muyu Hu. 請馳問寶虛實 is his request to ride to learn the facts about Bao. The direction north comes in the next unit.

proposals.before: Yu Hu requested to gallop and inquire into Murong Bao's truth and falsehood, and Murong De wept as he sent him.
proposals.after: Muyu Hu asked to ride swiftly and ascertain Murong Bao's actual circumstances. Murong De shed tears and sent him.
proposals.reason: The surname in 慕輿護 is Muyu. 問寶虛實 concerns the truth about Bao’s circumstances, and 德流涕而遣之 makes De the one who weeps and sends him.

proposals.before: He led hundreds of picked men north with Zhao Si plotting to murder Murong Bao.
proposals.after: He led several hundred picked men north after Zhao Si and plotted to kill Murong Bao.
proposals.reason: 隨思而北 says that the leader followed Zhao Si north. The following plot is narrated in the same sequence. Retaining the pronoun avoids inserting a personal name absent from this unit or assigning the plot to Zhao Si.

proposals.before: Yu Hu then led several hundred stalwarts and followed Zhao Si northward and plotted to kill Murong Bao.
proposals.after: He then led several hundred brave men north after Zhao Si and plotted to kill Murong Bao.
proposals.reason: The Chinese has no overt name for the subject of 乃率. The preceding unit names Muyu Hu. Keeping the subject pronominal avoids the added “Yu Hu” while preserving the following of Si, the direction north and the plot against Bao.

proposals.before: Yu Hu found no sign of Murong Bao, seized Zhao Si, and came back.
proposals.after: Muyu Hu found no sign of Murong Bao, seized Zhao Si, and came back.
proposals.reason: 護 is the shortened reference following 慕輿護 in s0091. Since the existing English uses a full name here, it should carry the complete surname.

proposals.before: When Yu Hu arrived he saw nothing, seized Zhao Si, and returned.
proposals.after: When Muyu Hu arrived he saw nothing, seized Zhao Si, and returned.
proposals.reason: The literal field expands 護 to a full name. The full name in s0091 is Muyu Hu, a spelling already used in s0123 and s0178.

proposals.before: It also hugs the Yangzi and Huai; waterways reach Jun, and in autumn and summer rains turn a thousand li into lakes.
proposals.after: It also lies close to the Yangzi and Huai rivers. Its waterways are open and deep, and prolonged rains in autumn and summer turn a thousand li of country into a lake.
proposals.reason: 水路通浚 describes the waterways. Neither this clause nor the parallel English field supplies evidence for a place named Jun. 秋夏霖潦 describes prolonged rains and flooding in autumn and summer.

proposals.before: It also hugs the Yangzi and Huai; waterways reach Jun, and in autumn and summer rains turn a thousand li into lakes.
proposals.after: It is also very near the Yangzi and Huai. The waterways are open and deep. With prolonged rains and flooding in autumn and summer, a thousand li become a lake.
proposals.reason: 水路通浚 describes the waterways. Neither this clause nor the parallel English field supplies evidence for a place named Jun. 秋夏霖潦 describes prolonged rains and flooding in autumn and summer.

proposals.before: Murong De summoned Bi Lü Hun in Qi commandery; when he refused, Murong Zhong attacked with twenty thousand men.
proposals.after: Murong De sent envoys to persuade Bi Lü Hun, governor of Qi Commandery. When Hun refused to comply, De sent Murong Zhong to attack him with twenty thousand infantry and cavalry.
proposals.reason: 遣使喻 makes De send an envoy to Hun. It does not say he summoned Hun. The Chinese identifies Hun as governor, then gives his refusal and the second order to Zhong to lead infantry and cavalry.

proposals.before: Taking Langye, Murong De drew over a hundred thousand from Xu and Yanzhou and forty thousand more north of Langye.
proposals.after: Murong De advanced and occupied Langye. More than a hundred thousand from Xu and Yan joined him, and more than forty thousand people north of Langye came to welcome him.
proposals.reason: The two groups perform different actions. 附 describes the first group joining De, and 迎者四萬餘人 records more than forty thousand who came to welcome him. The current idiomatic field reduces both to numbers De drew. The literal field already records the welcome.

proposals.before: The rebel Bi Lü Hun's father Wei once joined Duan Kan blocking chaos on the Zi River; the grand preceptor marched east and extirpated the wicked life.
proposals.after: The rebel Bi Lü Hun's father Wei once joined Duan Kan in rebellion at Zichuan. The grand preceptor's eastern campaign put an end to that rebel's life.
proposals.reason: The proclamation accuses Wei of joining Duan Kan in rebellious resistance at Zichuan. It attributes his death to the Grand Preceptor’s eastern campaign. Zizhi Tongjian 100 records that Wei was wounded and had already died when Ke sent someone to look for him. The wording does not require a personal killing by the Grand Preceptor.

proposals.after: The rebel Bi Lü Hun's father Wei once joined Duan Kan in rebellious resistance at Zichuan. The Grand Preceptor campaigned east, and the wicked man's life was cut short.
proposals.reason: The proclamation accuses Wei of joining Duan Kan in rebellious resistance at Zichuan. It attributes his death to the Grand Preceptor’s eastern campaign.
